blocks.text: Reach for a queue when **the order things arrive in is the order they must be handled**. In practice that shows up as four signals. Spot one, and a queue is almost always part of the answer.
1. Handle things in the order they arrive

Print jobs, requests to a web server, orders in a shop, messages between two programs: each must be handled **fairly**, oldest first. A queue also **absorbs bursts** — when work arrives faster than it can be done, it waits in line instead of being lost or reordered.

blocks.alt: A producer on the right adds new jobs at the back of a queue holding job 1, job 2 and job 3. A consumer on the left always takes the oldest job, job 1, from the front.

elements.text: bursts wait in line: nothing is lost or reordered
elements.originalText: bursts wait in line: nothing is lost or reordered

blocks.text: **Breadth-first search** explores everything **one step** away before anything **two steps** away. A queue gives exactly that order: nodes are handed out in the order they were discovered. That's why BFS finds the **shortest path** in an unweighted graph or grid, and why a tree's **level order** traversal uses a queue.

blocks.alt: A tree with root 1, children 2 and 3, and grandchildren 4, 5 and 6. A queue hands the nodes out in the order they were found: 1, then 2 and 3, then 4, 5 and 6 — level by level, nearest first.

elements.text: in the order they were found:
elements.originalText: in the order they were found:

blocks.caption: A queue drives a level order traversal: each round empties one level and enqueues the next.

blocks.text: 3. Keep only the recent past (a time window)

When items **expire in the order they arrived** — the last 100 log lines, the requests in the last minute — a queue holds exactly the live ones: new items join at the back, and expired ones fall off the front. A classic example is **Number of Recent Calls**: each `ping(t)` records a request at time t (times only grow) and returns how many requests arrived in the last 3000 ms, `[t − 3000, t]`.

blocks.alt: At ping 3002 the window is 2 to 3002. The queue holds 1, 100, 3001 and 3002. 1 is older than 2, so it leaves from the front; 100, 3001 and 3002 stay, so the answer is 3.

elements.text: 1 < 2: too old, it leaves from the front
elements.originalText: 1 < 2: too old, it leaves from the front

blocks.text: The loop never empties the queue — the ping just added is always inside its own window. Every time joins once and leaves at most once, so each ping costs **O(1) amortized**.

blocks.caption: Watch old pings fall off the front as the window slides forward.

blocks.text: To share something fairly, give the front item one turn, then send it to the **back**: dequeue, work, enqueue. Operating systems share the CPU between programs this way, in small time slices, and the same move solves puzzles like **hot potato** (next lesson).

blocks.alt: Round robin. The queue holds A, B, C. A, at the front, runs for one time slice and then joins the back, so the queue becomes B, C, A.

elements.text: A runs for one time slice...

blocks.text: When a queue is the wrong tool

items: **The newest item matters most** — undo, matching brackets, "the last thing I opened": use a **stack**.
**The most urgent item goes first**, not the oldest: use a **priority queue** (a heap).
**You need to look things up or reach the middle**: use an **array** or a **hash map** — a queue only shows its front.
**You add or remove at both ends**: use a **deque**.
Calls to a support line are answered in the order they came in. — **Queue**: first come, first served.
A browser's Back button returns to the page you were just on. — **Stack**: the newest page first.
The fewest knight moves from one square to another. — **Queue**: breadth-first search.
A hospital sees the most serious case first. — **Priority queue**.
The largest of the last k numbers, again and again. — **Deque**: the sliding window maximum.
Use a queue when items must be handled **in the order they arrived**.
**Breadth-first search** is a queue: nearest first, so it finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
A queue holds a **time window**: new items join at the back, expired ones leave from the front.
Dequeue, work, enqueue again = **round robin**, a fair way to take turns.
